paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ξενοφῶν ἐν τέλει τῶν Ἀπομνημονευμάτων τὸν Σωκράτους βίον ἐξετάζει. οὐ μόνον τὸν θάνατον διηγεῖται, ἀλλὰ πῶς ὁ ἀνὴρ ἔζη καὶ πῶς τοὺς συνόντας ὠφέλει. ἔγραφεν ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης εὐσεβὴς καὶ δίκαιος εἴη, καὶ τῶν ἡδονῶν ἐγκρατὴς γένοιτο. ταῦτα ἐπαίνου λόγοι εἰσίν· τὸν δὲ ἀναγνώστην δεῖ καὶ τὰ τεκμήρια τῆς κρίσεως ἀναμιμνῄσκεσθαι.

Περὶ τῆς πρὸ τῆς δίκης συνουσίας ὁ Ἑρμογένης αὐτῷ διηγήσατο. ἔλεγεν ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης οὐκ ἀγνοοίη τὸν κίνδυνον, ἀλλὰ τὸν βίον ἱκανὴν ἀπολογίαν νομίζοι. ὁ Ἑρμογένης ἠρώτησε πῶς οὕτως ἔχοι καὶ εἰ τῶν δικαστῶν ἐπιμελοῖτο. ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης ἀπεκρίνατο ὅτι περὶ τούτων ἤδη ἐσκεμμένος εἴη. τὸν λόγον τοῦ φίλου ὁ συγγραφεὺς παρέλαβεν.

Ἐν δὲ τῷ λόγῳ οὐ πάντα τὰ ῥήματα ἀλλάττειν ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν. ὁ συγγραφεὺς ἔλεγεν ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης δίκαιός ἐστιν· ὁ συγγραφεὺς ἔλεγεν ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης δίκαιος εἴη. ἀμφότεροι οἱ λόγοι δυνατοί, ἀλλὰ τὴν μορφὴν διαφέρουσιν. τὸ δὲ ἔλεγεν αὐτὸν δίκαιον εἶναι οὐ τῷ αὐτῷ τρόπῳ μεταβάλλεται. τὸ εἶναι τὸν αὐτὸν χρόνον πρὸς τὸ λέγειν δηλοῖ.

Ὁ Ξενοφῶν ἔλεγεν τὸν Σωκράτη τοὺς φίλους ὠφεληκέναι. ἡ ὠφέλεια πρὸ τοῦ λόγου γέγονεν, τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἔτι πρὸς τὴν κρίσιν διαφέρει. ἔγραφεν αὐτὸν μετὰ τὴν κρίσιν θαρροῦντα φαίνεσθαι. ἐνταῦθα δεῖ σκοπεῖν τίς ὠφέλησε, τίς ἔγραψε, καὶ πρὸς τίνα χρόνον ἕκαστον λέγεται. ὁ ἀκριβὴς ἀναγνώστης οὐ τὰς καταλήξεις μόνον ἀριθμεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὰς πράξεις συνάπτει.

Ἐκ τούτου πρὸς ἕτερον τοῦ Ξενοφῶντος βιβλίον τρεπόμεθα. ἐν τοῖς Ἑλληνικοῖς περὶ τῆς τῶν Ἀθηναίων διαλλαγῆς ἔγραψεν. ἔλεγεν ὅτι οἱ πολῖται τοῖς ὅρκοις ἐμμένοιεν. οὐκ ἔλεγεν ὅτι οὐδεὶς πρότερον ἠδικήκει, ἀλλὰ ὅτι κοινῇ ζῆν ἐπειρῶντο. οὕτω καὶ βίον καὶ πόλιν κρίνοντες ζητοῦμεν ποῖα ἔργα τὴν πίστιν βεβαιοῖ καὶ ποῖοι λόγοι μόνον εὐπρεπεῖς φαίνονται.

Ὁ Κῦρος τὸ χρήσιμον τῷ δικαίῳ συνέχεεν· οἱ κύριοι τῆς οἰκίας τὴν ἐπιμέλειαν ἐζήτουν· οἱ στρατιῶται τὸν στρατηγὸν ἔκρινον. ἐν τῇ πόλει ὁ μὲν νόμος φυλακὴν παρεῖχεν, ὁ δὲ φόβος αὐτὴν ἀφῄρει. ταῦτα οὐ μία ἱστορία ἐστίν, ἀλλὰ πολλὰ παραδείγματα ἐκ διαφόρων βιβλίων. ἕκαστον δεῖ πρὸς τὸν τόπον καὶ τὸν χρόνον καὶ τὸν λέγοντα ἀναφέρειν.

Τί οὖν περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς λέγομεν; ἐνταῦθα τὸν τρόπον καὶ τὴν προαίρεσιν ἐξετάζομεν, οὐ λόγους περὶ ἀθανασίας τῷ Ξενοφῶντι προστίθεμεν. ἡ ψυχὴ ἐν ταῖς πράξεσιν ἐξετάζεται· πῶς χρώμεθα τῇ δυνάμει, τίνα ἀκούομεν, καὶ ποίας αἰτίας δεχόμεθα; εἰ μὲν μόνον τοὺς φίλους ἐπαινοῖμεν, οὐκ ἂν δικαίως κρίνοιμεν. ἐὰν δὲ τὰ τεκμήρια σκοπῶμεν, βελτίους κριταὶ γενησόμεθα.

Τέλος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κρίσιν ὁ μαθητὴς γράφει. δύο παραδείγματα αἱρείσθω καὶ τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἀκριβῶς δηλούτω. οὐ δεῖ πάντα τῷ Ξενοφῶντι συγχωρεῖν, ἀλλὰ δεῖ πιστῶς ἀναφέρειν ἃ λέγει. οὕτως ὁ λόγος οὐ μόνον τῆς γλώττης ἄσκησις γίνεται, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς κρίσεως. ἡ μάθησις τελευτᾷ, ἡ δὲ ζήτησις τοῦ δικαίου ἔτι μένει.

reading.translation:
At the end of the Memorabilia Xenophon examines Socrates’ life. He tells not only of his death, but how the man lived and benefited his companions. He wrote that Socrates was pious and just and had become master of pleasures. These are words of praise; the reader must also recall the evidence for the judgment.

Hermogenes told him about the conversation before the trial. He said that Socrates was not unaware of the danger, but regarded his life as a sufficient defense. Hermogenes asked how this could be and whether he was taking the jurors into account. Socrates replied that he had already considered these matters. The writer received his friend’s account.

In reporting, it is not necessary to change every verb. The writer said that Socrates is just; the writer said that Socrates was just, with an optative. Both reports are possible, but differ in form. “He said that he was just,” using an infinitive, does not change in the same way. The infinitive indicates time simultaneous with the reporting.

Xenophon said that Socrates had benefited his friends. The benefit occurred before the report, and the deed still matters for the judgment. He wrote that Socrates appeared confident after the verdict. Here we must consider who benefited others, who wrote, and to what time each statement refers. A careful reader does not merely count endings, but connects actions.

From this we turn to another work of Xenophon. In the Hellenica he wrote about the Athenians’ reconciliation. He said that the citizens abided by their oaths. He did not say that no one had previously done wrong, but that they were trying to live together. Thus, in judging both a life and a city, we ask which deeds confirm trust and which statements merely look attractive.

Cyrus confused usefulness with justice; household owners sought careful management; soldiers judged their general. In the city law offered protection, but fear removed it. These are not a single history, but many examples from different works. Each must be related to its setting, time, and speaker.

What, then, do we say about the soul? Here we examine character and choice; we do not add arguments about immortality to Xenophon. Character is examined through actions: how do we use power, whom do we hear, and what explanations do we accept? If we praised only our friends, we would not judge justly. If we examine the evidence, we shall become better judges.

Finally the learner writes a judgment of their own. Let them choose two examples and make the evidence clear. One need not concede everything to Xenophon, but must report faithfully what he says. Thus the account becomes an exercise not only in language but in judgment. The course ends, but the inquiry into justice remains.

sections.title: 1. Secondary sequence in connected reporting
body: Historical reporting frames such as ἔλεγεν and ἔγραφεν can introduce an oblique optative in place of an original finite indicative or subjunctive. Present δίκαιός ἐστι becomes δίκαιος εἴη; an original deliberative τί ποιήσω; can become ἠρώτα τί ποιήσειε. The shift places the claim within a past report without erasing its original temporal relation.

Retention is also possible: ἔλεγεν ὅτι δίκαιός ἐστιν. A narrative can retain one clause and shift another. Explain the actual construction instead of treating variation as an error. Primary-to-secondary rewriting is therefore not a global replacement of every verb ending.

sections.title: 2. Infinitives and participles retain relative time
body: An infinitive report remains nonfinite after a historical reporting verb: ἔφη τὸν Σωκράτη ὠφελεῖν/ὠφελῆσαι/ὠφελήσειν. These are simultaneous, prior, and subsequent relative to the past report. ὠφεληκέναι presents a completed action with its relevant result. None must become an optative merely because ἔφη is past.

Participles retain their own agreement and aspect: ἔγραφεν αὐτὸν θαρροῦντα φαίνεσθαι, “He wrote that he appeared confident.” Map the accusative subject of φαίνεσθαι and the agreeing participle. Relative time is anchored to its governing construction, not automatically to the date on which the modern reader opens the page.

sections.title: 3. Nested speakers, questions, and negation
body: In ἔγραφεν ὅτι ὁ Ἑρμογένης ἔλεγεν ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης δίκαιος εἴη, distinguish writer, informant, and subject of the judgment. A pronoun can otherwise seem to jump between them. Use repeated names in your translation when needed, while preserving the source’s attribution.

Indirect questions require the same care: ἠρώτα εἰ ἐσκεμμένος εἴη, “He asked whether he had considered it.” The perfect participle agrees with its subject and the optative of εἰμί supplies the historical reporting form. Keep a negative inside the clause it denies. “He said that he did not know” is different from “He did not say that he knew.”

sections.title: 4. Cumulative translation: form, argument, and evidence
body: Read a sustained passage twice. First identify the argument, work, speaker, and chronology. Then bracket its clauses and annotate unfamiliar forms. Use subjunctive and optative signals, conditional systems, articular infinitives, absolute constructions, verbal adjectives, and perfect aspect to explain how the argument is built. Glossed exposure is support, not a demand to reproduce untaught paradigms.

For the final translation, write connected English that preserves attribution and distinctions in time. Recheck pronouns, negation, and argument structure before polishing style. In the accompanying reflection cite two course episodes and distinguish what the author records from what you infer. sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Memorabilia
body: At the end of Book 4, Xenophon gathers his assessment of Socrates into a closing portrait. Read the praise with the earlier encounters still in view. The final lesson returns separately to civic reconciliation in the Hellenica, inviting a comparison between character and institutions. That comparison is our course’s synthesis, not a claim that the two works form a continuous narrative.

Think of the four books as a gallery of encounters rather than a continuous biography. Book 1 answers accusations against Socrates and presents his religious practice and daily conduct. Books 2–3 explore family, friendship, useful work, and leadership. Book 4 gives sustained attention to education, including the questioning of Euthydemus. The movement from an ordinary habit to a public responsibility is characteristic of the collection.

Xenophon writes as an advocate for a teacher condemned at Athens in 399 BCE. His Socrates improves other people through example, questions, and practical reasoning. That organizing purpose makes the work valuable evidence for an ancient interpretation of Socrates; it does not make every conversation a stenographic record. Notice who asks the questions, who changes position, and where the narrator supplies the judgment.

Reading invitation: open Book 1, chapter 5, then Book 4, chapter 5. Ask whether mastery of appetite is merely a rule about pleasure or a condition for learning and dependable action. Keep a small dossier of the different kinds of evidence Xenophon offers: reported speech, observed habit, analogy, and the narrator’s praise.
Support your final evaluation with particular actions and arguments, rather than relying on the closing praise alone.

sections.title: A closing portrait is an argument
body: Memorabilia 4.8 ends with Xenophon’s assessment of Socrates. The praise gathers piety, justice, self-command, and practical benefit into a coherent portrait. It is the conclusion of a defense, not an independent grade assigned by an observer without commitments.

Ask which earlier episodes support the portrait and which questions remain open. A source’s admiration is itself evidence about remembrance. It is not a reason to discard the source, nor does it require the reader to accept every judgment without examining the examples.

sections.title: A gallery of justice
body: Revisit five scenes: Cyrus and the coats; the household’s labor; the soldiers’ hearing; civic reconciliation; and Socrates before the jurors. Name the work and the source status of each. The sequence is thematic, not a continuous biography, and its characters do not all inhabit the same time or political setting.

The return to Hellenica 2.4.43 asks how a city sustains trust after conflict. A person’s conduct and a city’s arrangements can both be judged through evidence, but they are not identical objects. Individual self-control cannot by itself replace institutions or procedural protection.

sections.title: Soul, character, and the limits of comparison
body: The title “Justice and the Soul” concerns character and ethical life in this final Xenophon lesson. Plato’s Phaedo supplies a distinct inquiry into the soul’s immortality, introduced in Lesson 47’s Culture/History page. Do not attribute those arguments to Xenophon merely because both authors remember Socrates.

Make a course-wide guide to genres: historical narrative, Socratic recollection, household dialogue, political dialogue, educational portrait, and defense. Explain how a work’s genre and purpose affect the questions you ask of it. A speech inside a history and a whole dialogue do not give identical kinds of access to the past.

sections.title: The final translation and reflection
body: After the new secondary-sequence instruction, translate the complete final reading as sustained prose. Work first without opening individual glosses, mark uncertainties, then consult support and revise. Retain a short record of three important revisions: one about speaker reference, one about aspect or relative time, and one about a clause relationship.

Complete the cumulative practice and final quiz, then write a short reflection comparing two works. State a claim about justice, cite an episode from each, and acknowledge one limit of the evidence. You may disagree with Xenophon. Accurate translation, grammatical explanation, and responsible use of sources—not agreement with a preferred moral verdict—are the criteria.

sections.title: Supported unseen translation — a final transfer task
body: This is a new course composition, not a quotation or additional historical evidence. Translate the whole passage before looking at the model below. Mark main verbs, bracket subordinate clauses, identify the speaker in each report, and explain one conditional and one perfect construction. Submit it as an additional section of your Lesson 48 reading translation.

Μετὰ τὴν στάσιν οἱ πολῖται ἐβουλεύοντο πῶς τὴν πόλιν σῴζοιεν. ὁ μὲν ἔλεγεν ὅτι πολλὰ κακὰ πεπόνθασιν, ὁ δὲ ἠρώτα εἰ τοῖς ὅρκοις ἐμμένοιεν. πρεσβύτης δέ τις ἔφη· «οἶδα ὅτι χαλεπόν ἐστι τοῖς πρότερον πολεμίοις πιστεύειν. ἐὰν δὲ μηδεὶς τοὺς νόμους φυλάττῃ, οὐδεὶς ἀσφαλὴς ἔσται. μὴ οὖν ὀργῇ μόνον κρίνωμεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ δίκαια σκοπῶμεν.» ταῦτα ἀκούσαντες οἱ παρόντες οὐκ εὐθὺς ὡμολόγουν. ἕκαστος γὰρ τῶν παλαιῶν κακῶν ἐμέμνητο. τέλος δὲ ἔδοξεν αὐτοῖς τοὺς ὅρκους φυλάττειν, ἵνα οἱ νέοι μὴ τὰ αὐτὰ πάθωσιν. οὐ γὰρ ἱκανὸν ἦν λέγειν ὅτι εἰρήνη γέγονεν· ἔδει καὶ ἔργῳ τὴν πίστιν βεβαιοῦν.

Help: στάσις = civil conflict; σῴζοιεν = might preserve (oblique optative); πεπόνθασιν = they have suffered; ἐμμένοιεν = would abide (here in an indirect question); ἀσφαλής = safe; ὡμολόγουν = they agreed; ἐμέμνητο = he remembered (pluperfect with past-state meaning); ἔδοξεν αὐτοῖς = they decided; πάθωσιν = may suffer; βεβαιοῦν = to confirm.

Assessment guide (20 points): main events and argument, 6; reporting, pronouns, and clause relationships, 6; tense, aspect, mood, and condition, 4; coherent English and explained revisions, 4. More than one English wording can earn full credit. The instructor evaluates the translation separately from the automatically scored final quiz.

questions.answer: After the civil conflict the citizens deliberated about how they might preserve the city. One said that they had suffered many evils, while another asked whether they would abide by their oaths. An older man said: “I know that it is difficult to trust those who were formerly enemies. But if no one observes the laws, no one will be safe. Let us therefore not judge by anger alone, but also consider what is just.” After hearing this, those present did not agree at once. Each remembered the former troubles. At last they decided to keep their oaths, so that the young might not suffer the same things. For it was not enough to say that peace had come about; they also had to confirm trust through action. The retained indicative πεπόνθασιν and oblique optative ἐμμένοιεν illustrate different choices within historical reporting; the future condition uses ἐάν plus subjunctive and a future result.
